home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits in Montréal: EnerGuide evaluations, costs and rebates
home-energy-audit.description: Book an EnerGuide home energy audit in Montréal: 3 licensed organizations, local prices, Quebec rebates and what 86% pre-1991 housing means for your upgrade list.
home-energy-audit.lede: 3 NRCan-licensed service organizations deliver EnerGuide home evaluations in Montréal. Here's what one costs, what it tends to find in Montréal houses, and which Quebec rebates it unlocks.

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Montréal homes
sections.html:
Of Montréal's 221,340 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 48% were built before 1961 and 86% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical Montréal house dates from 1961–1970, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Montréal gets about 4,028 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −22.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Mctavish. That's right around the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the evaluation's ranked list matters more in some cities than others.

In the Montréal area, 54% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards, 15% with a heat pump, 10% with a forced-air furnace and 6% with a boiler and radiators; electricity is the main heating energy for 71% of households, natural gas for 5% and oil for about 2% (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.

In Quebec, EnerGuide evaluations are booked through the provincial Rénoclimat program: the pre-retrofit evaluation costs $150 plus taxes, reimbursed when you receive financial assistance under the program, and the first post-retrofit evaluation is free.

• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating in gigajoules per year and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

sections.h2: Why air leakage matters in Montréal
sections.html:
Montréal gets about 4,028 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −22.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Mctavish. That's right around the middle of the 70 cities we cover.

Of Montréal's 221,340 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 48% were built before 1961 and 86% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older houses usually test leakier than newer ones, and an EnerGuide report compares your result with homes of the same era, so you can see whether your house is typical or a problem.

• Combustion safety. In the Montréal area, the main heating energy is natural gas for 5% and oil for about 2% of households. A tighter house changes how fuel-burning appliances vent, so the spillage check should be repeated after serious air sealing. Combustion safety testing in Montréal
  • Radon. Sealing shifts the pressure balance between the house and the soil. Health Canada's 2012 survey found 6.9% of 73 homes tested in the Région de Montréal health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 17.4% (1 in 6) of houses at or above the guideline for Montréal Metro Area (Montréal CMA). Test before and after big air-sealing jobs. Radon testing in Montréal

A blower door test is part of every EnerGuide evaluation rather than a separate purchase. In Quebec, EnerGuide evaluations are booked through the provincial Rénoclimat program: the pre-retrofit evaluation costs $150 plus taxes, reimbursed when you receive financial assistance under the program, and the first post-retrofit evaluation is free.

• A calibrated fan is fitted into an exterior door and pulls air out until the house is at 50 pascals, the standard test pressure.
  • The result is air changes per hour at 50 Pa (ACH50): how many times an hour the whole volume of air would leak out and be replaced at that pressure.
  • While the fan runs, you and the advisor walk the house and feel for leaks at the attic hatch, rim joists, pot lights, trim and plumbing and wiring penetrations.
  • A second test after the work shows what changed, and it is what most rebates pay on.

heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in Montréal: sizing a heat pump for −22.3°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280 room-by-room heat loss calculation for Montréal homes, sized to the local −22.3°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −22.3°C for Montréal, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Mctavish.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Montréal
sections.html:
−22.3°C is the 28th-coldest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −22.3°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

In the Montréal area, 54% of households heat mainly with electric baseboards, 15% with a heat pump, 10% with a forced-air furnace and 6% with a boiler and radiators; electricity is the main heating energy for 71% of households, natural gas for 5% and oil for about 2% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

ventilation-assessment.description: Why Montréal homes get window condensation and musty air, what a ventilation and humidity assessment measures, and when an HRV or ERV makes sense. 8% of local houses were built since 2001.
ventilation-assessment.lede: Condensation on windows, musty basements and stuffy bedrooms are ventilation and humidity problems, and they're easy to confuse with insulation problems. A ventilation assessment measures which one you have.

sections.h2: Why Montréal homes get humidity problems
sections.html:
Montréal gets about 4,028 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −22.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Mctavish. On Montréal's coldest days, window glass and poorly insulated corners get cold enough for condensation at humidity levels that feel normal indoors, so winter humidity needs to stay at the lower end of the comfortable range.

Of Montréal's 221,340 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 48% were built before 1961 and 86% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Newer houses (8% of Montréal's were built since 2001) are tight and usually have an HRV or ERV that needs balancing and cleaning. Older houses that get air-sealed can lose the accidental ventilation they used to rely on.

• Relative humidity in living areas and the basement.
  • Actual airflow from bath and kitchen fans, and whether they vent outside rather than into the attic.
  • How much fresh air the house gets, and whether an HRV or ERV is balanced.

attic-insulation-inspection.lede: The attic is usually the cheapest big energy fix in a house, and the inspection decides how to do it: how much insulation is there, where air leaks through the ceiling, and whether anything up there must not be disturbed.

sections.h2: What inspections find in Montréal attics
sections.html:
Of Montréal's 221,340 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 48% were built before 1961 and 86% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Attics in older houses commonly have a fraction of today's recommended insulation, and top-ups done over the years often buried air leaks instead of sealing them first.

Montréal gets about 4,028 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −22.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Mctavish. That's right around the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The colder the climate, the faster added attic insulation pays for itself.

Vermiculite. Loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold insulation may contain asbestos. Health Canada's advice is not to disturb it; have it sampled before any attic work. Asbestos and vermiculite testing in Montréal

sections.h2: The right order for the work
sections.html:
• Seal the air leaks first: top plates, pot lights, plumbing stacks, the hatch.
  • Fix ventilation baffles so new insulation doesn't block soffit vents.
  • Then top up the insulation. Burying unsealed leaks under new insulation wastes much of the benefit.

What an attic inspection checks.

radon-testing.title: Radon testing in Montréal: local levels, test kits and certified professionals
radon-testing.description: Radon in Montréal: Health Canada survey results for the Région de Montréal region (6.9% above the guideline), how to test for 3+ months, where to get kits and C-NRPP professionals locally.
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 6.9% of homes tested in the Région de Montréal health region were above the guideline, and the only way to know about your house is to test it.

sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 6.9% of 73 homes tested in the Région de Montréal health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 17.4% (1 in 6) of houses at or above the guideline for Montréal Metro Area (Montréal CMA).

The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests and more of them were taken in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

• Use a long-term test of at least three months, with most of it in the heating season, which gives the most conservative result.
  • Place the detector in the lowest level you spend four or more hours a day in, away from drafts, and follow the kit's instructions.
  • If the result is above 200 Bq/m³, Health Canada recommends fixing it within a year, sooner if it's much higher.

Our full radon testing guide.

• The Association pulmonaire du Québec sells long-term detectors for about $50 including analysis, and some municipal libraries lend electronic monitors.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your Montréal postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

• Quebec's construction code requires a soil-gas barrier in new dwellings and, since April 17, 2025, a passive radon exhaust stack.
  • The Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 toward mitigation for households with low to moderate incomes or a lung cancer diagnosis.
  • If your level is high, mitigation (usually a sub-slab depressurization fan system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional) typically costs $2,000–$4,000.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in Montréal?
faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 6.9% of 73 homes tested in the Région de Montréal health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 17.4% (1 in 6) of houses at or above the guideline for Montréal Metro Area (Montréal CMA). Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least three months, with most of it during the heating season. Short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in Montréal?
faq.a: The Association pulmonaire du Québec sells long-term detectors for about $50 including analysis, and some municipal libraries lend electronic monitors. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits for about $30–$60.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Typically $2,000–$4,000 for a sub-slab depressurization system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional.

carbon-monoxide-testing.title: Carbon monoxide testing in Montréal: the Quebec alarm rules and appliance checks
carbon-monoxide-testing.description: CO safety for Montréal homes: what Quebec law requires, why it matters with 5% of households heating with natural gas, where alarms go and how appliances get checked.
carbon-monoxide-testing.lede: Carbon monoxide is odourless and can kill. Quebec has no province-wide rule requiring CO alarms in existing houses: provincial rules cover larger multi-unit buildings, and for houses it's up to each municipality's by-law, so ask your local fire service.

sections.html: Quebec has no province-wide rule requiring CO alarms in existing houses: provincial rules cover larger multi-unit buildings, and for houses it's up to each municipality's by-law, so ask your local fire service.

In the Montréal area, the main heating energy is natural gas for 5% and oil for about 2% of households (Statistics Canada, 2023). Any fuel-burning appliance, fireplace or attached garage is a potential CO source.

Single-detached houses make up 7% of Montréal's households; many have an attached garage, another reason to put an alarm near the door into the house.

• Alarms next to sleeping areas and on every storey, tested monthly and replaced by their end-of-life date (usually 7 to 10 years).
  • Annual service of fuel-burning appliances by a licensed technician.
  • A combustion spillage test during an energy evaluation, which catches a venting problem before it produces CO.

Our carbon monoxide guide · Combustion safety testing in Montréal

faq.q: Are carbon monoxide alarms mandatory in Montréal?
faq.a: Quebec has no province-wide rule requiring CO alarms in existing houses: provincial rules cover larger multi-unit buildings, and for houses it's up to each municipality's by-law, so ask your local fire service.

faq.q: Where should CO alarms go?
faq.a: Outside every sleeping area and on every storey, following the manufacturer's instructions. Some rules also call for one near a fuel-burning appliance or the door from an attached garage.

faq.q: How long do CO alarms last?
faq.a: Most have an end-of-life date of 7 to 10 years printed on the unit; replace them by then even if they still beep when tested.

mold-testing.h1: Mold and air quality testing in Montréal
mold-testing.title: Mold testing in Montréal: air quality sampling and finding the moisture source
mold-testing.description: Mold and indoor air quality testing in Montréal: when sampling is worth $300–$600, why cold winters cause condensation, and how to find an accredited lab.
mold-testing.lede: Mold sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mold problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure.

sections.h2: Why mold shows up in Montréal homes
sections.html:
Montréal gets about 4,028 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −22.3°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Mctavish. On cold days, exterior corners, closets on outside walls and window frames get cold enough for condensation, which is where mold usually starts in Montréal houses.

Of Montréal's 221,340 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 48% were built before 1961 and 86% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

• You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

If you can see mould, you usually don't need a test to know it's there; you need to fix the moisture and clean it up properly.

Quebec has a voluntary standard for handling mould in homes (BNQ 3009-600, 2020); no province has a mandatory residential mould standard.

Ask any Montréal tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in Montréal · Our mold and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: How much does mold testing cost in Montréal?
faq.a: Plan on about $300–$600 for a typical sampling visit (a September 2026 planning range); lab fees for extra samples add to that.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

asbestos-testing.h1: Asbestos and vermiculite testing in Montréal
asbestos-testing.title: Asbestos testing in Montréal: vermiculite, labs and the Quebec rules
asbestos-testing.description: Asbestos and vermiculite testing in Montréal, where 86% of houses were built before 1991: what to sample, lab costs and the Quebec rules for renovation.
asbestos-testing.lede: About 190,100 Montréal houses (86%) were built before 1991, when asbestos still turned up in insulation, flooring, plaster and duct wrap. A lab test before renovation is the only way to know.

sections.h2: Where asbestos shows up in Montréal houses
sections.html:
Of Montréal's 221,340 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 48% were built before 1961 and 86% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.
  • Vinyl floor tiles and their adhesive, textured ceilings and some plaster.
  • Duct wrap and pipe insulation on older heating systems.

In Quebec, CNESST rules require contractors to check for asbestos before any work that could release dust, and the province tells homeowners to have suspect materials checked by a qualified contractor or an IRSST-recognized lab and never to do asbestos work themselves. Quebec treats material as asbestos-containing from 0.1% asbestos, a stricter line than most provinces.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program or recognized by the IRSST in Quebec.

Our asbestos and vermiculite guide · Attic inspections in Montréal

faq.q: Do I need an asbestos test before renovating in Montréal?
faq.a: If the house was built before 1991 and the work will disturb insulation, flooring, plaster or duct wrap, test first. In Quebec, CNESST rules require contractors to check for asbestos before any work that could release dust, and the province tells homeowners to have suspect materials checked by a qualified contractor or an IRSST-recognized lab and never to do asbestos work themselves. Quebec treats material as asbestos-containing from 0.1% asbestos, a stricter line than most provinces.

faq.q: How much does asbestos testing cost?
faq.a: About $50–$150 per lab sample, plus the assessor's visit. Abatement, if needed, is quoted separately.

faq.q: What should I do if I have vermiculite in the attic?
faq.a: Leave it alone, keep the attic closed, and have it sampled before any attic work. Health Canada advises against disturbing it or removing it yourself.

lead-paint-testing.title: Lead paint testing in Montréal: which homes are at risk and how to test
lead-paint-testing.description: 48% of Montréal's houses were built before 1961, when lead paint was common. How to test with $15–$40 swabs or a lab, and how to renovate safely.
lead-paint-testing.lede: Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably has lead paint somewhere. That's 48% of Montréal's houses (built before 1961, per the 2021 Census), plus exterior paint on many of the 38% built from 1961 to 1990.

sections.h2: Which Montréal homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of Montréal's 221,340 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 48% were built before 1961 and 86% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

Don't dry-sand, use a heat gun or power-wash it. Contain the work area, mist surfaces, clean with a HEPA vacuum, and keep children and pregnant people away until cleanup is done. No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. and Yukon must include lead in pre-renovation or demolition hazard inspections.

faq.q: Does my Montréal house have lead paint?
faq.a: If it was built before 1960, probably; 1960–1990, possibly on the exterior. Test the surfaces you plan to disturb.

faq.q: Are lead test swabs reliable?
faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

faq.q: What does lead paint testing cost?
faq.a: Swab kits run about $15–$40; lab analysis and XRF testing cost more and are quoted by the firm.

There's no free provincial service: send samples to a lab accredited by Quebec's environment ministry (the CEAEQ list), which supplies the bottles. The ministry recommends testing for bacteria at least twice a year, in spring and fall, plus a chemical analysis while the well is in use.

  • Nitrate, especially near farmland or septic systems.
  • Metals and naturally occurring contaminants such as arsenic, uranium or manganese when a well is new and every few years after, depending on local geology.

faq.q: How often should I test my well?

commercial-energy-audit.title: Commercial energy audits in Montréal: reporting rules and incentives
commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in Montréal: ASHRAE levels, 2 reporting rules that apply, and 4 utility or government incentives for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in Montréal: 2 mandatory reporting rules and 4 incentive programs we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in Montréal
sections.html:
• Règlement 21-042 sur la divulgation et la cotation des émissions de GES des grands bâtiments (in force): 2,000 m2 (21,528 sq ft) or larger, or 25+ dwelling units (phased: 15,000 m2+ non-residential and City-owned 2,000 m2+ from 2022; 5,000 m2+ and 50+ units from 2023; 2,000 m2+ and 25+ units from 2024). Source
  • Règlement sur la déclaration obligatoire de la performance environnementale de certains bâtiments (Loi sur la performance environnementale des bâtiments, chapitre P-9.02) (in force - first declarations due June 30, 2027): From Jan 1, 2027: buildings of 5,000 m2+ (not exclusively residential), residential or partly residential buildings with 50+ units, and buildings owned by public bodies other than municipal bodies (buildings under 100 m2 excepted, subject to a metering condition in the text). From Jan 1, 2028: buildings of 2,000 m2+ (not exclusively residential) and residential buildings with 25+ units. Source

• Efficient Solutions Program - Energy Analysis component (Hydro-Québec): Pays for eligible costs of an energy analysis (including in-house labour): 40% of eligible costs when the report is accepted and 60% after at least one measure is implemented (up to 100% in total). Caps for energy-efficiency analyses: existing buildings with 1-2 GWh reference use, $8,000 + $12,000 ($20,000 total), analysis must identify at least 100,000 kWh/yr of savings; over 2 GWh, $20,000 + $30,000 ($50,000 total), at least 200,000 kWh/yr. Analyses that also cover demand-response measures: up to $60,000 ($24,000 + $36,000 for buildings over 2 GWh). Details
  • ÉcoPerformance - Analyse de mesures de réduction des GES (Gouvernement du Québec (MELCCFP)): Standard analysis (energy study, fuel-switching study, fugitive-emissions study): 50% of eligible expenses, max $25,000 per site for small/medium energy users (under 36,000 GJ/yr non-electric) or $75,000 for large users. Complex analysis: 75%, max $100,000 / $300,000. Paid 50% on the signed purchase order and the rest after the engineer-signed report is accepted; project must finish within 24 months. Details
  • Energy audit and implementation - Feasibility Study grant (Énergir): 50% of the pre-tax cost of a feasibility study, max $50,000. Follow-on implementation grant: $1 per m3 of natural gas saved in the first year (max $1,000,000 per account), plus up to $15,000 for energy tracking. Details
  • Recommissioning of mechanical systems grant (Énergir): Investigation phase: 75% of eligible costs; implementation: $1 per m3 of gas saved up to 75% of eligible costs (measures with payback over 1 year); transfer and continuous-monitoring phases: 75% of eligible costs. Up to $100,000 per project in total. Details

• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.

faq.q: Do Montréal buildings have to report energy use?
faq.a: Yes, above certain sizes: Règlement 21-042 sur la divulgation et la cotation des émissions de GES des grands bâtiments; Règlement sur la déclaration obligatoire de la performance environnementale de certains bâtiments (Loi sur la performance environnementale des bâtiments, chapitre P-9.02).

faq.q: Are there incentives for commercial energy audits in Montréal?
faq.a: Yes: Efficient Solutions Program - Energy Analysis component; ÉcoPerformance - Analyse de mesures de réduction des GES; Energy audit and implementation - Feasibility Study grant; Recommissioning of mechanical systems grant. Check eligibility and pre-approval rules before you commission the audit.

faq.q: What does a commercial energy audit cost?
faq.a: It depends on the building's size and the ASHRAE level. Get quotes that state the level and the deliverables.
